will be avenged. The quality of the work done will suffer if a
man thinks less of the matter itself than of the impression
which he wishes to create on other people. We need hardly
be reminded that there are men who from the urge to gain
recognition undertake senseless and mad things, with the
sole object of increasing their own sense of merit; just as there
are children who, being incapable of doing anything useful,
will do stupid and impudent things merely to draw atten-
tion to themselves.
Again, this lack of sincerity and objectivity goes hand in
hand with a spirit of lovelessness. Men who are hungry for
recognition may indeed compel respect and admiration for
their accomplishments, but not love. Because they are
concerned to win admiration from others, they in fact isolate
themselves from others and make genuine friendship and
fellowship impossible. When they take other people into
account they do so in order to compare themselves with their
fellows and to measure themselves against them with the
object of strengthening the feeling of their own superior worth.
Such a man becomes envious when he sees that others can
do better than himself; he becomes arrogant and despises
those to whom he thinks himself, in virtue of his achieve-
ments, superior. It is clear that true human society is ruined
by this spirit. For community life flourishes only when the
one freely appreciates the merits of the other and does not
attempt to assert his own superiority, when each rejoices in
the good which he sees in other people, gladly learns from
them what can be learnt, gladly recognizes superior value
wherever it is found. The man for whom other people serve
only as a foil to set off his own sense of value becomes
unjust, disputatious, harsh and unloving. He then resembles
the portrait of the Pharisee who says: "I thank Thee, God,
that I am not like other men!" We certainly feel that we
should not like to have such people as friends. Do we wish to
become such people ourselves?
